claims.claim: RFC-001 offers the Kubernetes audit trail as the accountability guarantee for impersonation, answering that audit events capture both the actual user and the impersonated user; T-28695 establishes that only the sync path honors the AppProject's destinationServiceAccounts while Server-Side Diff runs as the cluster credential from the cluster Secret. The guarantee therefore covers sync only: every server-side apply dry-run issued to compute a diff is authorized and recorded as the standing cluster credential with no impersonation headers, so an auditor reconstructing who acted on a resource sees the impersonated ServiceAccount for writes and the control-plane credential for every diff, and whoever reviews destinationServiceAccounts is reviewing an identity that never appears on the diff path.

The recorded root cause for the CI diff failures and the ticket that analyses the same error disagree about which identity performs the diff. note-1 root-causes T-26271 as 'with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch on cluster-scoped stuff'; T-28695 states the opposite mechanism, that the diff path does not honor destinationServiceAccounts and runs as the cluster credential, which is consistent with T-26271's own log naming user system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server. The two root causes imply opposite remediations (grant patch to the destination ServiceAccount versus make the diff path impersonate), and note-1's rollout gate, which holds the per-project impersonation flag closed 'until the diff story is fixed', is anchored to the version T-28695 contradicts.

T-9095 is an open access request asking Argo CD to honor the RBAC already configured for a user or group for actions like resource deletion and pod exec, so cluster RBAC becomes the single reviewed control. RFC-001 is the design that converges on that access model, but it declines it in two named ways: its design considerations defer impersonating users or groups ('support to impersonate users or groups can be added in future'), and the service account is determined per Application from the AppProject's destinationServiceAccounts entry matching the destination, not from the requesting principal. Governance consequence for the pair: if RFC-001 ships, the identity that acts remains a destination ServiceAccount, the Kubernetes audit trail names that ServiceAccount rather than the human who clicked, and access review stays on AppProject configuration held by Argo CD admins instead of the cluster RBAC that T-9095's requesters already administer, leaving the duplication T-9095 asks to remove.

T-27833 needs a per-resource identity split: the Application should bootstrap the namespace under the Argo CD control-plane service account while the impersonated ServiceAccount, stripped of permission on kind: Namespace, performs the sync. RFC-001 forecloses that shape, stating that 'the service account to be used for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than on per resource level' and that Application.spec.destination.namespace selects one service account for all resources in the Application. The control gap T-27833 documents therefore survives impersonation: the AppProject deny policy on Namespace and the clusterResourceWhitelist watch the Argo CD API/UI identity, while the acting identity for a namespace committed to git is the application controller, so a namespace that omits the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label is applied with no denial recorded on the reviewed control.

Enabling impersonation narrows the sync identity but does not retire the privileged credential it was meant to replace. RFC-001's Example 3 relies on the argocd-manager service account with cluster-admin privileges that `argocd cluster add` creates in kube-system, keeping it as the cluster-config credential for control-plane operations. T-28695 shows that same standing cluster credential is exactly the identity the diff path acts as, and that it accretes real patch authority one resource kind at a time because RBAC has no dry-run verb, five rounds so far. So the credential the feature was designed to demote is still held by the control plane and is gaining write authority over more kinds as charts are added, while the least-privilege boundary the design claims applies only to sync.

T-28695 states that the safety of the diff path's unbounded patch grant 'rests on Argo CD's convention of always sending dryRun=All, not on any enforced boundary', and flags #24134 to make Server Side Diff the default. RFC-001's mitigation for privilege escalation is that only admins configure the sync service account at the AppProject level and that administrators can restrict impersonation targets via the resourceNames field in the RBAC spec. Neither control touches the diff path, which does not impersonate: the evidence an auditor would need after Server-Side Diff ships as a default is proof that the granted patch rules were only ever exercised in dry-run, and no such record exists because the API server authorizes the patch before the dry-run flag is evaluated.

RFC-002 makes the hydrator push to git under a repository-write Secret holding a githubAppPrivateKey, and places the authorization check in-process ('it's the application controller's job to ensure that the user has write access to the repo before making the call'), so the actor recorded on the git side of every hydrated commit is the GitHub App, not the developer. T-28239 completes the picture on the signature side: one cluster-wide signing key, per-project keys explicitly out of scope, so every hydrated commit in every project carries the same GPG identity, and the project's SourceIntegrity policy verifies only that. Human authorship survives solely as the commitAuthor and commitMessage fields RFC-002 templates into README.md and hydrator.metadata, which are unsigned payload rather than verified provenance.

RFC-002's security considerations state that the git push secrets 'will need to be stored in a namespace separate from the other Argo CD components to provide a bit extra protection'. T-28239 mounts the hydrated-commit signing key from a Secret in the Argo CD namespace, cluster-wide, and pairs it with the operator adding the public key to argocd-gpg-keys-cm and the project's SourceIntegrity policy. The credential that makes a commit trusted for the hydrated branch therefore lives in the namespace RFC-002 wanted it out of: anyone holding read on Secrets in the Argo CD namespace can produce commits the SourceIntegrity policy accepts as hydrator output, and because the key is cluster-wide there is no per-project blast radius or per-project rotation.

T-27327 proposes that rollback, in both hydrator modes, write directly to the sync branch and bypass the staging branch, on the reasoning that single-application rollbacks 'don't fit into existing promotion flows'. RFC-002 designates push-to-stage precisely as the integration point where an external system moves changes to the deployment branch. Combining them: rollback becomes a route to change deployed state that never traverses the promoter, executed under the hydrator's repository-write credential, so the reviewer that push-to-stage inserted is absent exactly for the operation performed under incident pressure, and the only record is a commit authored by the commit server's identity.

T-28239 specifies fail-fast signing with no silent fallback: with commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits enabled the commit server refuses to push any commit it cannot verify against the configured key, and the branch is enforced by the project's SourceIntegrity policy. T-27327's rollback is described as a plain git checkout/commit/push sequence against the sync branch. If rollback is implemented outside the commit server's signing path, every rollback commit is unsigned and rejected by the same SourceIntegrity policy that protects the hydrated branch, so signing enforcement and rollback fail together at the moment rollback is needed.

The PRD's Non-Goals record that a user setting the custom deletion strategy gets 'a configuration field that accepts input but ignores it silently', while the strategy document states that the UI/CLI/API cannot manage the deletion order of child applications at all and that teardown remains a manual operator action performed one Application at a time. An auditor inspecting an ApplicationSet whose strategy carries deletionOrder: Custom would read it as evidence that an ordered teardown control is in force; the controller applied no such order, no error surfaced, and nothing in the spec or event stream records the divergence. The declared configuration is the only artifact, and it is not evidence of the behavior.

The PRD's Security Considerations conclude that 'no additional roles or privileges are needed to be able to delete deployed applications in a specific order, so no impact on the security aspects of Argo CD workloads'. note-2 establishes the operating reality: the incident runbook requires an operator to switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before hand-deleting any child app, a privileged edit to the ApplicationSet strategy performed under incident pressure, and note-2 itself observes there is no controller-level check or alert behind it. The change therefore does move who acts and under what authority: incident responders need write on ApplicationSet specs, the only evidence the mode was switched before a manual deletion is the Kubernetes audit record of that patch, and the only control is the runbook.

T-29001's Option 1 places per-cluster QPS and Burst limits in the Cluster Secret's metadata.annotations, and Option 2 inside its data.config alongside the bearerToken. T-28695 identifies that same Cluster Secret credential as the identity Server-Side Diff acts as and the one accreting patch grants. Making the Secret a routine performance-tuning surface widens who needs write access to the object holding the cluster credential, from credential custodians to whoever tunes throughput for edge clusters, and neither document proposes a review path that distinguishes an annotation edit from a credential edit.
